parole.significato: A proposed but unadopted air-officer rank of the Royal Air Force equivalent to air vice-marshal.
parole.testo: A compounding of the Scottish Gaelic àrd (“chief”) + eun (“bird”).

parole.significato: A professional poet and singer, like among the ancient Celts, whose occupation was to compose and sing verses in honor…
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1449. From Scottish Gaelic bàrd, from Old Irish bard, from Proto-Celtic *bardos (“bard, poet”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“praise”), and reinforced by Latin bardus, borrowed from Celtic. Cognate with Latin grātus (“grateful, pleasant, delightful”), Sanskrit गृणाति (gṛṇāt

parole.significato: A type of boat used especially in the Hebrides and West Highlands of Scotland in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic bìrlinn, from Old Norse byrðingr.

parole.significato: A design of smaller streetcar with a single four-wheel truck produced in North America between 1915 and 1930, and appar…
parole.testo: Scottish habitational surname from a place in Morayshire, probably from Scottish Gaelic braonach (“misty, wet, damp”).

parole.significato: A hobgoblin.
parole.testo: Modification of Scottish Gaelic bodach (“old man, churl, miser, ghost”), from Middle Irish botach (“serf, rustic, peasant”), from bot (“penis”) + -ach.

parole.significato: boor, oaf, bungler
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic bumalair.

parole.significato: The larva of a botfly, which infests the skin of various mammals, producing warbles, or the nasal passage of sheep, or…
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly a modification of Scottish Gaelic boiteag (“maggot”), but the word already existed in Middle English, so the reverse direction of borrowing is likely. Possibly from Middle Low German [Term?].

parole.significato: The standard of a Highland clan.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic bratach, from Old Irish bratach; see brat (“cloak, mantle”).

parole.significato: A tartan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic breacan.

parole.significato: A pointed instrument, such as a joiner's awl.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic bròg. Compare brob.

parole.significato: A rabbit, especially a juvenile one.
parole.testo: From bun (“rabbit”) + -y (diminutive suffix). Probably from Scottish Gaelic bun (“bottom, butt, stump, stub”), from Old Irish bun (“the thick end of anything, base, butt, foot”), from Proto-Celtic *bonus, though its origin is uncertain. Compare also English bum. Together with rabbit, bunny has large

parole.significato: A long, thick log held upright at one end and tossed in the Highland games.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic cabar (“spar, pole”).

parole.significato: The game of shinty.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic camanachd, from caman (“shinty stick”). Cognate with Irish camánacht.

parole.significato: A British breed of domestic duck developed at Uley, in Gloucestershire, England, at the turn of the 20th century.
parole.testo: * As a Scottish surname, from Scottish Gaelic Caimbeul, from cam (“crooked”) + beul (“mouth”). Compare Cameron, from Scottish Gaelic cam (“crooked”) + sròn (“nose”). * As an Irish surname, from Mac Cathmhaoil (“son of Cathmhaol”), see Caulfield, Cowell. * As an English surname, variant of Camel, pro

parole.significato: Left-handed.
parole.testo: Northern and Scottish dialects from Scottish Gaelic caerr (“awkward”) + handed.

parole.significato: The crooked spade; an implement of tillage peculiar to the Highlands, used for turning the ground where a plough cannot…
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic cas-chrom.

parole.significato: A type of foot plough with a crooked spade component, used in the Scottish Highlands.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic, from cas (“foot”) + crom (“crooked, bent”).

parole.significato: A Highlander working as a professional fighter; a mercenary attached to a Scottish clan.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic ceatharn (“troop”), ceathairne (“peasantry, yeomanry”).

parole.significato: To attend a ceilidh (noun sense 1).
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Scottish Gaelic cèilidh (“a pilgrimage; a social call, visit; a sojourn; a social gathering with dancing, etc., ceilidh”) and Irish célidhe (archaic), céilí (“a social call, visit; a social gathering with dancing, etc., ceilidh”), both from Old Irish célide (“social call, v

parole.significato: A small village or hamlet, especially in the Highlands or Western Scotland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic clachan.

parole.significato: A small triangular wire-strung harp of Gaelic origin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic clàrsach (“harp”) by the 1810s, possibly from clàr (“board, plank; table”). The word is cognate with Irish cláirseach (“harp”).

parole.significato: The Scottish broadsword used during the Early Modern period.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic claidheamh beag (literally “small sword”). First attested in 1825 as Clay-beg.

parole.significato: A dirge or lamentation.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic corranach and Irish corānach.

parole.significato: A bowl-shaped geographical feature formed by glaciation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic coire.

parole.significato: A fishing-boat.
parole.testo: First attested in 1722; perhaps from the Scottish Gaelic cobhan (“coffer”, “box”, “ark”).

parole.significato: A traditional Scottish dessert made with whipped cream, whisky, oatmeal, honey, and raspberries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic crannachan.

parole.significato: A fiery cross used as a rallying cry in the Scottish Highlands.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic crann-tara.

parole.significato: An obsolete Scots unit equal to 4 ploughgates, notionally comprising 400 Scottish acres.
parole.testo: Scottish Gaelic dabhach (“vat, large unit of land”); the "land unit" sense may reflect substrate influence on Gaelic from Pictish.

parole.significato: A kind of spindle, around which the cord is rolled as it is made, afterwards being slipped off the end by removing the…
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic dealgan (“spindle”).

parole.significato: Clockwise, sunwise.
parole.testo: From 1771, from Scottish Gaelic deiseil, deiseal (“southward, sunward; clockwise”) (adjective and adverb), from Old Irish dessel (“sunwise”), from dess (“right, south”) and sel (“turn”).

parole.significato: A glass or metal double-walled flask for holding a liquid without much loss or gain of heat; a vacuum bottle or thermos…
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic deòradh (“pilgrim, stranger”), an occupational surname for a custodian of holy relics. It could also be an habitational surname, from Dewar, Scottish Borders. The flask is named for James Dewar, who is credited with its invention.

parole.significato: A Scottish honey-flavoured whiskey liqueur.
parole.testo: Supposedly from Scottish Gaelic an dram buidheach (“the satisfying drink”).

parole.significato: A gentleman from the Scottish Highlands.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic duine (“man”) plus Scottish Gaelic uasal (“noble”).

parole.significato: A pen for enclosing sheep, mainly in the Scottish Highlands.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic fang, from Scots fank, perhaps ultimately related to archaic fang (“to seize, catch”).

parole.significato: A young sea trout, in the year after they return to fresh water after their smolt migration stage.
parole.testo: A possible anglicisation of Scottish Gaelic fionnag (“young salmon”). Compare fionnag (“whiting”), a calque of English whiting, from fionn (“white”).

parole.significato: One of a breed of beef-producing cattle, originating in Galloway, Scotland.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic (eadar na) Gall-Ghàidhealaibh (literally “(among the) foreign Gaels”), a term used for Gaelic-speaking Norse settlers.

parole.significato: A kind of small horse originally bred in Galloway, Scotland.
parole.testo: From Galloway, Scotland, where they were bred.

parole.significato: A small and usually disdained type of horse, typically bred in Scotland and Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic gearran, Irish gearrán.

parole.significato: A male attendant of a Scottish Highland chief.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic gille (“helper”), from Middle Irish gilla (“youth, young man; boy, male child; messenger, page, servant”), possibly borrowed from Old Norse gildr (“brawny, stout; of full worth”). Compare Irish giolla (“boy”).

parole.significato: A brimless cap, longer than it is wide, and creased lengthwise across the top, often with ribbons trailing behind, and…
parole.testo: From Glengarry, a valley in northern Scotland, from Scottish Gaelic Gleann Garaidh (“valley of the River Garry”).

parole.significato: The entrails or offal of a dead deer, especially when removed. Also the entrails of other wild animals, when removed.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic grealach (“entrails”), from Proto-Celtic *gre-lach, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer- (“bowels”).

parole.significato: A United States fifty-dollar bill.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic Grannd, from Anglo-Norman graunt (“big, large”), from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grand. The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of Ulysses S. Grant featured on it.

parole.significato: Pre-eminence; victory or superiority in combat (hence also, the prize for winning a combat).
parole.testo: From (pre-reform) Scottish Gaelic gré, from Old Scottish Gaelic gray.

parole.significato: solan goose or northern gannet
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic guga.

parole.significato: mouth of a river; confluence
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic inbhir (“river mouth, confluence”), from Old Irish *in(d)ber, from Proto-Celtic *endo-ber-o (“carrying in”), from *endo (“in”), from Proto-Indo-European *en-do-, from *h₁én. Analogous to Welsh aber (“river mouth, confluence”), from Old Welsh oper, aper, from Proto-Brythonic.

parole.significato: A whole wheel or ball of cheese.
parole.testo: 15th century, from Scottish Gaelic càbaig.

parole.significato: Red chalk; ruddle.
parole.testo: Probably from Scottish Gaelic cìl (“ruddle”).

parole.significato: A pencil of black lead.
parole.testo: Compare Scottish Gaelic cìl (“ruddle”).

parole.significato: A malevolent shapeshifting spirit, most often in the form of a horse, believed to haunt the rivers and lochs of Scotlan…
parole.testo: Possibly from Scottish Gaelic cailpeach or colpach, meaning "colt"; recorded earliest in a placename (Kelpie hoall, Kirkcudbrightshire) in 17th century. The dog breed, from 1889, derives from the name shared by the first two breeding bitches (dam and pup) in Victoria, Australia, which in turn derive

parole.significato: A closely woven broad bonnet, having a peak of the same material at the top, originally made at Kilmarnock.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic, from cill (“churchyard, chapel”) + the Saint name Marnock. The name is from Mo-Ernin-og (“my little Ernan”).

parole.significato: A narrow arm or channel of the sea between an island and the mainland, or between two islands.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic caol (“narrow; thin; firth, narrows, strait, kyle; narrow part of something”) (genitive singular form caoil), from Old Irish coíl (“narrow, slender”), from Proto-Celtic *koilos (“thin”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect; to split”).

parole.significato: One of a breed of small Highland cattle.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic gaidhealach (“Gaelic, Highland”); see Gàidheal.

parole.significato: A pool of water, especially one formed and agitated by the water from a cascade.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic or Irish linn (“pool, pond”), or else a Brythonic source such as Cumbric *lınn, all from Proto-Celtic *lindos (“lake, liquid”). Conflated to some extent with linn (“waterfall”).

parole.significato: An area of uncultivated ground near a village or farmhouse.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic lòn (“marshy meadow”) (compare lèana (“wet meadow, marsh, meadow”)).

parole.significato: A lake.
parole.testo: From Middle English lough, borrowed from Scottish Gaelic loch. Doublet of lay, Looe, and lough.

parole.significato: A small loch (lake)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic lochan, diminutive of loch (“lake”).

parole.significato: A single-masted ship propelled by oars, usually indicating a Scottish title associated with islands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic long-fhada (“galley”, literally “long ship”).

parole.significato: An evergreen tree, of the genus Macadamia, native to Australia and cultivated in Hawaii.
parole.testo: From the genus name Macadamia, coined by the German-Australian botanist Ferdinand von Mueller in 1857, in honor of John Macadam, whose surname is an alternative spelling of MacAdam, from Scottish Gaelic Mac Àdhaimh (“Adam's son”). By surface analysis, Mac- + Adam + -ia.

parole.significato: A type of calcareous sandy terrain formed mostly from seashells, found by the coast in areas of Scotland and Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic machair.

parole.significato: A brand of personal computer manufactured by Apple Inc.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic Mac an Tòisiche, meaning "son of the thane (Old Irish toísech (“leader”))". The brand is named after McIntosh, an apple cultivar, in turn also from the Scottish Gaelic name.

parole.significato: A United States five-hundred-dollar bill.
parole.testo: Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaoich, "son of Fionnlaoch (=Fair Warrior)". The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of William McKinley featured on it.

parole.significato: Synonym of rakehoe.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic MacLeòid (“son of Leòd”), from Old Norse Liótr (“the Ugly (one)”), from Old Norse ljótr (“ugly, scary”). The combination tool was created in 1905 by Malcolm McLeod, a US Forest Service ranger.

parole.significato: A festival of Scottish Gaelic song, arts and culture, akin to the Welsh eisteddfod.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic mòd.

parole.significato: The vocal imitation of instrumental music.
parole.testo: Calque of Scottish Gaelic puirt à beul (“tunes from a mouth”).

parole.significato: A person from the Scottish island of Mull.
parole.testo: Scottish Gaelic [Term?]

parole.significato: Any Scottish mountain having a height of more than 3,000 feet.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic * (mountains): Named after Scottish mountaineer Sir Hugh Thomas Munro.

parole.significato: An obsolete Scots unit equal to ¹⁄₈ daugh, notionally comprising 50 Scottish acres.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic ochdamh (“eighth”), from Old Irish ochtmad, from Proto-Celtic *oxtūmetos.

parole.significato: Expresses woe or sorrow.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English oghane, from Scottish Gaelic ochóin and Irish ochón. Cognate with Scots ochone.

parole.significato: A grandchild.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic ogha; for spelling see Scots.

parole.significato: A little kilt.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic fèileadh beag, from fèileadh (“wrap, fold”) + beag (“little”).

parole.significato: A series of musical variations for the bagpipes, usually martial or funerary in nature.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic pìobaireachd (“act of playing the bagpipes”), from pìobaire (“piper”) + -achd (“abstract noun suffix”).

parole.significato: A pad behind the saddle of a horse for a second rider.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic pillean (“little rug”), from Latin pellis (“animal skin, pelt”).

parole.significato: Covered in blotches or pimples.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic pluc.

parole.significato: Coregonus clupeoides, a species of freshwater whitefish endemic to Loch Lomond in Scotland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic pollan. Doublet of pollan.

parole.significato: Any of three species of small grouse in the genus Lagopus found in subarctic tundra areas of North America and Eurasia.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic tarmachan, of unknown origin. The pt- comes from a mistaken belief in a Greek origin, as if related to ptero- (“wing”).

parole.significato: A roll of fiber, used as a precursor to yarn.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic roileag (compare roll).

parole.significato: An English person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic Sasannach (“Saxon”).

parole.significato: A small, single-edged knife worn tucked into the hose (stocking) as part of traditional Scottish Highland dress along w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic sgian-dubh: sgian (“knife”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut; to cut off, sever”)) + dubh (“black; (figurative) hidden”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”)). The plural form sgianan dubha is also borrowed from Scottish Gaelic.

parole.significato: garbage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic sgudal.

parole.significato: A rocky peak in Scotland.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic sgùrr.

parole.significato: Synonym of slingshot.
parole.testo: From Scottish shangan, from Scottish Gaelic seangan, influenced by the Chinese city.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A noisy party or festivities.
parole.testo: Origin uncertain; perhaps an alteration of shindy, or from Scottish Gaelic sìnteag (“jump, leap”).

parole.significato: herring
parole.testo: Presumably from Scottish Gaelic sgadan.

parole.significato: A Skye terrier.
parole.testo: Derived from Scottish Gaelic An t-Eilean Sgitheanach, of long disputed (probably non-Indo-European substrate) origin, with several theories proposed and none widely accepted; see Etymology of Skye.

parole.significato: A distinctive phrase of a person or group of people (such as a movement or political party); a motto.
parole.testo: From earlier sloggorne, slughorne, slughorn (“battle cry”), borrowed from Scottish Gaelic sluagh-ghairm (“battle cry”), from Old Irish slóg (“army; (by extension) assembly, crowd”) + gairm (“a call, cry”). Slóg is derived from Proto-Celtic *slougos (“army, troop”), from Proto-Indo-European *slowgʰos

parole.significato: A small pouch, usually made of either fur or plain or fur-trimmed leather, which is worn, suspended from a belt or chai…
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic sporan (“purse”), from Middle Irish sparán, possibly from Late Latin bursa (“purse”), ultimately from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, “leather, hide”).

parole.significato: Plunder, especially cattle taken as booty.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic sprèidh (“cattle”).

parole.significato: An ancient divination method of the Highland Scots involving animal sacrifice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic taghairm, from Old Irish togairm, from Proto-Celtic *to-garrman, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵh₂r̥-smn̥, from *ǵeh₂r- (“to call, to shout”); compare Irish toghairm (“an invocation, a summons”), from gairm, gair (“to call; to invoke”), ultimately from the same Proto-Indo-E

parole.significato: second sight; the involuntary ability of seeing the future or distant events.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic taibhs.

parole.significato: A reward for information about the theft of cattle.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic taisgeal.

parole.significato: Trousers, especially if close-fitting and tartan.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic triubhas, from Middle Irish triubus.

parole.significato: A calfskin stuffed with straw and given to a cow, as if living, to induce her to give milk.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic tulachan.

parole.significato: A nosegay given by one person to another to convey a message in the language of flowers.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic tùs f (“nice smell, incense”) and debatable second part, a mere reduplication, or mùsg (“musk”) for a moschate flower, or mùisear (“primrose”).

parole.significato: The base theme of a piece of classical bagpipe music.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic ùrlar (“floor”).

parole.significato: A brownie in Scottish folklore.
parole.testo: From Scottish Gaelic ùruisg.

parole.significato: The body.
parole.testo: Clipping of body. The sense of “person” may alternatively derive from Scottish Gaelic bodach (“old man”) via Scots.

parole.significato: A heavy working shoe; a brogue.
parole.testo: An alteration of brogue. Most dictionaries give the source as Irish *brógán (from bróg (“shoe”) + -án (diminutive suffix)) or its Scottish Gaelic equivalent, but no such word can be confirmed to exist in either language (apart from the given name Brógán, the source of the surname Brogan).

parole.significato: A group of people all descended from a common ancestor, in fact or belief, especially when the exact genealogies are no…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish clann (“offspring, children of the family”) and Scottish Gaelic clann, both from Old Irish cland, borrowed from Old Welsh plant, itself borrowed from Latin planta (“shoot, offspring”). Doublet of plant and planta.

parole.significato: A long Scottish dagger with a straight blade.
parole.testo: Etymology unknown, apparently from Scots dirk. First attested in 1602 as dork, in the later 17th century as durk. The spelling dirk is due to Johnson's Dictionary of 1755. Early quotations as well as Johnson 1755 suggest that the word is of Scottish Gaelic origin, but no such Gaelic word is known. T

parole.significato: A small, rich, pastry or quick bread, sometimes baked on a griddle.
parole.testo: Originally Scots, possibly from Middle Low German schö̂ne (“fine flour bread”), or Middle Dutch schoonbroot (“fine bread; a kind of flat angular loaf”), from schoon (“fine”) + broot (“bread”). Alternatively, might derive from Scottish Gaelic sgonn (“lump, mouthful”).

parole.significato: A confrontation where authorities brutally repress those wanting civil rights, similar to Bloody Sunday in Selma, Alaba…
parole.testo: Taken to use in the 19th century when similar-sounding names, Elma, Thelma, Alma, Wilma, etc. were in vogue. Perhaps a shortening of Anselma, or from the name of a place in the James Macpherson's Ossian cycle of epic poems, itself from Scottish Gaelic sealladh + math (“good vision”). In some cases p

parole.significato: Whiskey or whisky.
parole.testo: [Alt: A glass with a round bottom which tappers to the lip, served with usquebaugh.] Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *wed- Proto-Indo-European *-r̥ Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥der.
